title: The costs you don't see
principle: Price minus stock cost isn't profit. Count every hidden cost.

screens.text: PepperTap delivered groceries in two hours across Indian cities and raised over $50 million. In April 2016, it shut grocery delivery down.

screens.prompt: By late 2015 it said it handled 20,000 orders a day. Why didn't more orders save it?

options.label: Each order cost more than it earned

screens.why: Its CEO said the cash burned on every order kept rising. Big discounts, and keeping two-hour delivery ready even on slow days, cost more than orders brought in.

screens.title: What one sale really leaves
screens.text: Margin is what one sale leaves you. So ask: what did this order leave after every cost it caused? Delivery, fees, ads and returns count.

screens.title: Riya's T-shirts
screens.text: Riya sells T-shirts online at ₹499. Each shirt costs her ₹180. She thinks she keeps ₹319 an order.

screens.prompt: Each order also costs ₹70 shipping, ₹15 packing, ₹10 payment fee and ₹150 in ads. What does Riya really keep?
screens.why: ₹319 − ₹70 − ₹15 − ₹10 − ₹150 = ₹74. The ads alone cost almost half her margin.

wrong.a: You left out one cost. Take off all four: ₹70, ₹15, ₹10 and ₹150.
wrong.c: That's price minus the shirt. The other costs come with every order too.

screens.prompt: 1 in 5 cash-on-delivery orders is refused at the door. That one wasted ₹150 ads, ₹15 packing, ₹140 shipping both ways. Profit on 5 orders?
screens.why: 4 good orders × ₹74 = ₹296. The refused one cost ₹150 + ₹15 + ₹140 = ₹305. ₹296 − ₹305 = −₹9. She works hard and loses money.

wrong.a: That's 5 × ₹74. But the refused order earned nothing and still cost money.
wrong.b: That's the 4 good orders. Now take off what the refused one cost.

screens.prompt: Put Riya's costs per order from biggest to smallest.
screens.why: The ad nearly matches the shirt. Online, the cost of finding a buyer is often the biggest cost after stock, and the easiest to forget.

screens.prompt: Riya can cut one cost by 20%. Which cut saves her most per order?
screens.why: 20% of ₹180 = ₹36. 20% of ₹150 ads = ₹30. 20% of ₹70 shipping = ₹14. A better supplier price beats a cheaper courier.

wrong.a: Close. 20% of ₹150 is ₹30, but 20% of the ₹180 shirt is ₹36.
wrong.b: 20% of ₹70 is only ₹14. Go for the biggest cost.

screens.prompt: A cloud kitchen sells biryani at ₹300 on a food app. Food costs ₹110, the app takes 25%, packing is ₹20. What's left?
screens.why: 25% of ₹300 = ₹75. ₹300 − ₹110 − ₹75 − ₹20 = ₹95. And that's before rent, gas and the cook's wage.

wrong.b: That's only price minus food and packing. The app's 25% is ₹75 more.
wrong.c: Check the app's cut: 25% of ₹300 is ₹75, not ₹55.

screens.prompt: Dal khichdi leaves ₹20 and sells 30 a day. Paneer bowls leave ₹45 and sell 18 a day. Which earns more per day?
screens.why: Khichdi: 30 × ₹20 = ₹600. Paneer: 18 × ₹45 = ₹810. A fast seller can earn less than a slow one. Count rupees per day, not plates.

wrong.a: More plates, but fewer rupees: 30 × ₹20 = ₹600 against 18 × ₹45 = ₹810.

screens.setup: The app offers to 'promote' the biryani for 10% more commission. It promises 40% more orders: 140 a day instead of 100.
screens.question: Each biryani leaves ₹95 now. Do you join?

options.label: Yes. 40 more orders a day is big
options.outcome: 10% of ₹300 is ₹30 more per order. 140 × ₹65 = ₹9,100 a day, against 100 × ₹95 = ₹9,500. You cook 40 more meals to earn ₹400 less.
options.why: You counted orders, not what each order leaves.
options.better: Work out what's left per order at the new commission before you sign.

options.label: Do the per-order sum first
options.outcome: You see ₹9,100 against ₹9,500. You offer to try it only if the extra cut is 5%: 140 × ₹80 = ₹11,200.
options.why: Every extra cost comes off each order. The sum shows when more sales mean less money.

options.label: Leave the app for good
options.outcome: You stop paying 25%, but your 100 orders a day drop to 20 walk-ins.
options.why: The app's cut is a cost, but it also brings the orders.
options.better: Price the deal per order, then decide.

screens.text: Count every cost that comes with ___ order, not just the ___.
screens.why: Shipping, ads, fees, packing and returns ride along with every order. Price minus stock is only the start.

summary: Price minus stock is only the start. Take off every cost that comes with each order.
Returns, ads and app cuts can turn a 'good' sale into a loss.
A fast seller can earn less than a slow one. Count rupees per day.

cards.front: Price ₹600, stock ₹300, delivery ₹80, ads ₹200. What's left per order?
Item A leaves ₹5 and sells 100 a day. Item B leaves ₹12 and sells 50. Which earns more a day?
cards.back: B: ₹600 a day. A: ₹500. Count rupees, not units.
